query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating in situ ultrasonic peening during a solid‐state friction stir deposition of mechanically alloyed AlCrFeNiSi powder can further reduce residual tensile stresses and enhance the mechanical properties of miniature components by inducing beneficial compressive surface stresses and additional microstructural refinement.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi powder produced by mechanical alloying to achieve a near-equiaxed, moderately dense microstructure with controlled particle size and flowability.
generation.intervention: Integrate an in situ ultrasonic peening module into the friction stir deposition process. Ultrasonic vibrations (at frequencies typical for peening treatments) are applied concurrently with layer deposition.
generation.conditions: Processing of miniature components (on the order of a few centimeters in at least one dimension) at solid‐state deposition temperatures (<500 °C) to avoid melting. Deposition parameters remain close to those used in conventional AFSD, with the additional ultrasonic peening activated during each layer build.
generation.structural_mediator: Induced localized plastic deformation at the deposited layer surfaces, leading to a thin compressively stressed layer and further grain refinement at the microstructure boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Friction stir deposition inherently reduces thermal gradients but can still leave residual tensile stresses due to cyclic plastic deformation. The superimposed ultrasonic vibrations generate rapid high-frequency impacts that plastically deform the surface, converting tensile stresses into compressive stresses and refining the grain structure further – thereby improving yield strength and fatigue resistance without invoking significant heat input that could coarsen grains.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to components made under conventional high-thermal-load AM or standard AFSD without peening, the integrated process will produce miniature AlCrFeNiSi parts exhibiting substantially lower overall residual tensile stresses, the presence of beneficial compressive surface stress layers, and improved mechanical properties (e.g., higher yield strength and fatigue performance) with simplified post-processing.
generation.baseline: Miniature additive manufactured components produced via conventional fusion-based AM or standard friction stir deposition (without ultrasonic peening), which typically suffer from higher residual tensile stresses and degraded mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for AlCrFeNiSi feedstock processed via friction stir deposition in miniature geometries where the processing temperature remains in the solid-state regime (below melting and recrystallization thresholds). Scaling effects in larger parts or deviations in powder characteristics might alter the outcomes.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends findings from friction stir deposition studies on similar high-entropy alloys (e.g., PMC11277587::web::000::abstract) and research demonstrating that ultrasonic peening converts tensile stresses into compressive stresses in laser AM parts (e.g., PMC6384986::web::000::abstract). The uncertainty lies in the novel integration of in situ ultrasonic peening with AFSD for AlCrFeNiSi, particularly regarding process synchronization, potential interference with deposition dynamics, and scale-dependent effects in miniature components.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components using friction stir deposition: one set with in situ ultrasonic peening integrated during deposition and one set using conventional AFSD without peening. Characterize both sets for residual stress distribution (using X-ray diffraction and EBSD misorientation mapping) and perform mechanical testing (tensile strength, fatigue life) under standardized conditions.
measurements: Residual stress profiles (quantitative XRD measurements of tensile vs. compressive stress values)
Grain size distribution and microstructural refinement (via SEM/EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ ultrasonic peening integration does not produce a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >20% reduction in residual tensile stress) or demonstrably improve mechanical performance (e.g., yield strength and fatigue life) compared to the conventional AFSD group, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

At heat-treatment temperatures of 225 and 250 °C, the residual stresses were increased and even exceeded the stresses in the as-built condition. This is theorized to be the result of magnesium in the phase Al3Mg2 dissolving into solution. Observation of the microstructure found that grain coarsening was present with increasing temperatures and times despite the low treatment temperatures. This negatively impacts the potential for Hall–Petch strengthening and further contributes to the diminishment of tensile strength. Exploration into the field of stress relief for AM-fabricated components is of considerable benefit, as these residual stresses have the potential to lead to part failure and dimensional warpage and negatively impact mechanical behavior. However, quantifying and eliminating these stresses is not straightforward due to the fabrication method’s complexity. AbstractAdditive friction stir deposition (AFSD) is an emerging solid-state additive manufacturing process with a high deposition rate. Being a non-fusion additive manufacturing (AM) process, it significantly eliminates problems related to melting such as cracking or high residual stresses. Therefore, it is possible to process reactive materials or high-strength alloys with high susceptibility to cracking. Although the residual stresses are lower in this process than with the other AM processes, depending on the deposition path, geometry, and boundary conditions, residual stresses may lead to undesired deformations and deteriorate the dimensional accuracy. Thermal cycling during layer deposition, which also depends on the geometry of the manufactured component, is expected to affect mechanical properties. To this day, the influence of the deposit geometry on the residual stresses and mechanical properties is not well understood, which presents a barrier for industry uptake of this process for large-scale part manufacturing. Ultrasonic peening treatment (UPT) has been proved to be an effective way of improving residual stresses distribution in weld structures. Thus, it shows a great potential in stress modification for metal parts fabricated by additive manufacturing technology. In this paper, an investigation into the ultrasonic treatment process of AlSi10Mg specimens fabricated by selective laser melting (SLM) process was conducted by means of experimental and numerical simulation. The specimens were prepared using a SLM machine, and UPT on their top surface was carried out. The residual stresses were measured with an X-ray stress diffraction device before and after UPT. Meanwhile, a finite element simulation method for analyzing the influence of UPT on the residual stress field of specimens was proposed and validated by experiments. Firstly, the thermal mechanical coupling numerical simulation of the SLM process of the specimen was carried out in order to obtain the residual stress distribution in the as-fabricated specimen.
